notes: \cpara{Quotes Daniel Dennett's essay (\textsc{Journal of Consciousness Studies}, 1995) on the one defence of zombies Dennett had seen: a descendant of Ned Block's lookup table. I could not reach a full text of the essay, so the quoted sentence is unchecked.}
\cpara{Explains a lookup table as programmers use the term. The example checks: two inputs from 1 to 100 give $100 \times 100 = 10{,}000$ entries.}

\cpara{Shows how fast such tables grow. The figure checks: 200 words, each one of 850, give $850^{200} \approx 7.6 \times 10^{585}$ conversations. LessWrong prints the exponent as a superscript; the plain text reads ``10585''.}
\cpara{Supposes a table for all of a brain's inputs and outputs: unreasonably large, but possible ``in principle''.}
\cpara{Grants that the table is not a zombie in the classic sense, since it is physically unlike a brain, and that it could not fit in our universe; the second point is set aside for the argument.}
\cpara{Asks the post's question, and defines the sense of ``zombie'' it uses: something that behaves exactly like a human without being conscious. See the note on the cellphone paragraph.}
\cpara{Gives the case for calling the table a zombie: from outside it behaves like a human.}
\cpara{Reports, with a hedge about the author's reading, that no one claims a lookup table is conscious, not even functionalists.}

\cpara{This is the use Ned Block made of the machine in ``Psychologism and Behaviorism'' (1981), against behaviorism about intelligence: ``the machine has the intelligence of a toaster'' (p.~21, as quoted by Drew McDermott, \textsc{Minds and Machines}, 2014). Shannon and McCarthy had raised the objection to Turing's test in 1956: a machine could look answers up in ``a suitable dictionary'' (as quoted by Gon\c{c}alves, 2024). The post credits Block only through Dennett's quotation.}
\cpara{States the apparent problem: the table looks like a ``Zombie Master'' (the term of ``Zombies! Zombies?''), an unconscious system that makes a body talk about consciousness.}
\cpara{Describes how little happens inside the table: a lookup, like balls rolling from a stored stack into a trough.}
\cpara{Gives the objection that brains are mechanical too: if ion channels can be conscious, why not levers?}

\cpara{Gives the functionalist's answer: the table has the wrong pattern of levers, with no beliefs about beliefs, no self-model and no memory. Haskell is a purely functional programming language, whose functions do not change stored values; the joke is that a conscious program must write to memory.}
\cpara{Poses the question the rest of the post answers: where do the table's papers about consciousness come from?}
\cpara{Introduces ``Follow-The-Energy'' through Feynman's father. The quotation matches Feynman's ``Judging Books by Their Covers,'' in \textsc{Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!}.}
\cpara{Notes that energy is conserved, so ``using up'' energy needs another account.}
\cpara{Names the grown-up version, following negentropy, and links the author's post on the second law.}

\cpara{Introduces the post's method, ``Follow-The-Improbability'': every improbable belief needs a matching amount of evidence. The rule is the one argued in the posts the paragraph links, such as ``How Much Evidence Does It Take?''}
\cpara{Compares an argument in which improbability appears from nowhere to a perpetual motion machine.}
\cpara{Gives an example: a belief in a cake in the asteroid belt, formed without evidence, is very unlikely to be true, though it cannot be proved impossible.}
\cpara{Adds that even naming one specific hypothesis needs evidence, because there are countless others (the point of ``Einstein's Arrogance'').}
\cpara{Restates the previous paragraph's rule in one sentence.}
\cpara{Applies the method: a table that matches a human is enormously improbable, so ask where it came from.}
\cpara{Concedes that this departs from standard practice, in which thought experiments ignore physical possibility, and says that here the table's origin matters.}
\cpara{First answer: the table was computed from a specification of a human brain.}

\cpara{Concludes that such a table is a relay, like a cellphone. Block made the same comparison in 1981, with a two-way radio: ``The two-way radio is like my machine in being a conduit for intelligence,'' and ``All the intelligence it exhibits is that of its programmers'' (pp.~21--22, as quoted by McDermott).}

\clogic{``A conscious algorithm'' assumes that a brain's specification, run on other hardware, is conscious. The previous post left that open (``the reasons shall have to wait for future posts''). The argument does not need it: the specification came from a human brain, so the talk traces back to a conscious human either way.}

\clogic{Here ``zombie'' changes sense. The post's question was: ``does it behave exactly like a human without being conscious?'' The post does not say the table is conscious: the cellphone it is compared to is not, and a few paragraphs later the post says ``The consciousness isn't in the lookup table.'' So in that sense the table is still a zombie. The cellphone answer is about where the table's talk comes from, which is the sense the anti-zombie principle needs.}
\cpara{Second answer considered: the table was generated at random.}

\cpara{States the many-worlds reading of quantum randomness as fact (``the deterministic result''); the book argues for that reading in its next sequence. The argument here does not need it. Under any interpretation, a table drawn at random matches a given human's with a probability of about 2 to the minus its length in bits, and ``where did the improbability come from?'' arises in the same way.}
\cpara{Recasts random generation as drawing one table from a bin of all possible tables, and asks again where the improbability came from.}
\cpara{If the table was picked by design, the picker is ``probably conscious'' and the table is again a relay, at two removes.}
\cpara{Draws the lesson: the consciousness is in whatever picked the table, not in the table or in the machine that made all possible tables.}
\cpara{Says the real source of a conversation is whatever accounts for its improbability, however far away, as the Sun drives the toy in Feynman's story.}
\cpara{The philosopher's last move: stipulate that the table was drawn by pure chance.}
\cpara{Answers that the improbability now comes from the philosopher's stipulation, outside the thought experiment.}
\cpara{Locates the consciousness in the philosopher, and in the readers' brains, which supply what the imagined table would say.}
\cpara{States the moral, with ``generally'': trace talk about consciousness back and you find consciousness. This is how the post connects the table to the Generalized Anti-Zombie Principle.}
\cpara{Applies the moral to the chatbot ``Zombie Master'' of ``Zombies! Zombies?'': the humans who wrote its source texts are conscious.}

\cpara{Extends it to a future program that talks like a confused philosopher without being conscious: its likeness to humans traces back to its conscious author. The post grants that such a program need not itself be conscious.}
\cpara{Returns to the case the thought experiment was built for: a table drawn by genuinely pure chance.}

\cpara{The answer is offered as opinion, and the two lines that follow give as its reason the reductio stated earlier. So the post allows that, if such a table were drawn, something would talk as we do without being conscious. What it disputes is that such talk ever arises without a conscious source, which is a claim about probability; the post flagged this move (``not standard philosophical procedure'').}

\cpara{Applies the same reasoning to AI: an AI that does improbably nice things needs an account of how its design was chosen, or the improbability is ``pulled out of nowhere.'' The people described are not named; they are reported from the author's experience.}
\cpara{Says that earlier posts on AI and morality were produced by the same method, before its rules were spelled out.}
\cpara{States the connection to the author's work on Friendly AI openly, as a joke about coincidence.}
